rows.title: USDA chief says agency is trying to fill key jobs after paying 15,000 to leave
rows.standfirst: Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins says the department will consider bringing back some employees who took the government's deferred resignation offer.

rows.title: Energy Star, efficiency program that has steered consumer choice, targeted in cuts
rows.standfirst: An Environmental Protection Agency plan to eliminate its Energy Star offices would end a decades-old program that gave consumers a choice to buy environmentally friendly electronics and save money on bills, consumer and environmental groups said.

rows.title: In the wake of tariffs, cargo at the Port of LA is down 35%
rows.standfirst: The immediate impact of the cargo decline affects virtually every business around the ports, but port officials say this downturn will soon be felt much more broadly.

rows.title: America's air traffic control problem
rows.standfirst: Newark Liberty International Airport has been a mess the past week, with hundreds of flights cancelled and hundreds more delayed. It was triggered in part by an incident on April 28, when air traffic controllers for the airport experienced a radar and communications blackout. They were unable to reach approaching planes.

rows.title: How a visit from actor Jon Voight led Trump to post about movie tariffs
rows.standfirst: Since he announced his intention to impose a 100% tariff on movies made outside of the United States, President Trump has hedged, saying he's open to meeting with industry leaders.

rows.title: What "Made in China" actually means
rows.standfirst: Virtually every product brought into the United States must have a so-called "country of origin." Think of it as the official place it comes from. And this is the country that counts for calculating tariffs.

rows.title: Disney's newest theme park will be in Abu Dhabi
rows.standfirst: The company's theme parks and cruises make up a fast-growing section of its profits. The new park will be located on Yas Island with a number of existing attractions.

rows.title: Cheap and easy ways to stock your emergency go bag
rows.standfirst: Putting together a go bag doesn't have to be daunting or expensive. Here's how to create a functional kit that doesn't require much money, time or effort.

rows.title: Kari Lake says OAN's far-right coverage will fuel Voice of America
rows.standfirst: Senior presidential adviser Kari Lake says Voice of America will rely on coverage from the far-right OAN network. OAN has offered unwavering support of President Trump.

rows.title: The Fed holds interest rates steady as Trump's tariffs spark uncertainty
rows.standfirst: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady Wednesday as President Trump's tariffs threaten to raise prices and drag down economic growth.

rows.title: Basic Fun! CEO warns tariffs could double toy prices, threaten Christmas sales
rows.standfirst: Toymakers say they will have to raise prices to offset Trump's tariffs. NPR's Michel Martin speaks with Jay Foreman, CEO of Basic Fun!, whose toys include Care Bears, Tonka Trucks and Lincoln Logs.

rows.title: U.S. and Chinese officials will meet in Geneva in first sign of thaw in trade war
rows.standfirst: The superpowers have been locked in a geopolitical blinking contest, waiting for the other side to reach out. The talks in Switzerland are the first concrete sign of a potential thaw in the deadlock.

rows.title: The fantasy vs. reality of Trump's "smokestack nostalgia"
rows.standfirst: The Trump administration wants their recent tariffs to function as incentives for Americans to produce more of our own goods in our own factories. And one poll shows that 80% of us say the country would be better off if more Americans worked in manufacturing. But why do people on both sides of the aisle want these jobs back so much? What have we lost culturally with the loss of factory jobs that we want to bring back? And ultimately - how does the fantasy of bringing more factory jobs back stack up against the reality of how American manufacturing works today? Brittany is joined by Vox senior correspondent Dylan Matthews and Montclair State University associate professor Jeffrey Gonzalez to find out.

rows.title: Why do shrimpers like tariffs?
rows.standfirst: Many businesses are scared of what President Trump's tariffs will mean for their industry. However, the shrimping industry is one that doesn't seem to be worried. In fact, shrimpers say they welcome them. On today's episode, why shrimpers are embracing the tariffs and whether economists agree that this tariff is good for Americans.

rows.title: WeightWatchers files for bankruptcy protection to eliminate debt burden
rows.standfirst: WeightWatchers said Tuesday it is filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection to eliminate $1.15 billion in debt and focus on its transition into a telehealth services provider.

rows.title: What happened to U.S. farmers during the last trade war
rows.standfirst: The U.S. exports billions of dollars worth of agricultural products each year — things like soybeans, corn and pork. And over the last month, these exports have been caught up in a trade war.

rows.title: What we misunderstand about gun violence
rows.standfirst: The U.S. is known around the world for its problem with gun violence. The vast majority of murders in the U.S. are committed using guns. But what leads one person to shoot another? The "conventional wisdom" says gun violence is usually the act of calculated criminals or people acting out of desperate economic circumstances. But economist Jens Ludwig believes the conventional wisdom is wrong. Today on the show, he explains why he believes many of us fundamentally misunderstand the problem of gun violence and how behavioral economics reveals some potential solutions.

rows.title: U.S. egg prices fall for the first time in months but remain near record highs
rows.standfirst: The average price for a dozen Grade A eggs declined to $5.12 last month after reaching a record $6.23 in March. It was the first month-to-month drop in egg prices since October 2024.

rows.title: ESPN's new streaming app could replace cable for some but may end up costing them more
rows.standfirst: ESPN says its subscription plan will cost $29.99 a month. An analyst says that, combined with subscriptions to other streaming services, could drive the cost up to the price of cable packages.

rows.title: President Trump's Trip to the Middle East
rows.standfirst: President Trump's first major overseas trip of his second term is to the same place as his first term, the Middle East. Trump is visiting the Gulf States of Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. And he is scheduled to meet with Syria's new president for the first time. We'll hear about the significance of that meeting and the deals between the U.S. and Gulf countries being announced. We'll also hear about the personal relationships and family business deals Trump has with various Gulf Arab rulers.

rows.title: UnitedHealth Group abruptly replaces CEO Andrew Witty, deepening a terrible year
rows.standfirst: The health care conglomerate is facing mounting financial problems – and ongoing consumer anger over high costs and denied claims.

rows.title: Inflation cools in April — but tariffs could upend the picture in coming months
rows.standfirst: Consumer prices in April were up 2.3% from a year ago, the smallest annual increase in more than four years. Grocery prices fell 0.4%, thanks to a large drop in the price of eggs.

rows.title: Importers respond U.S.-China tariff cuts. And, takeaways from day 1 of Diddy's trial
rows.standfirst: Importers are ready to get back to business after the U.S. cut tariffs on China, but uncertainty looms. And, media mogul Diddy's first day of trial held a slew of accusations.

rows.title: A major toy manufacturer is already nervous about Trump tariffs for holiday season
rows.standfirst: Jay Foreman, CEO of Basic Fun!, says the Trump administration's shifting tariff policy has created chaos for businesses — and could still disrupt the holiday season.

rows.title: Why an economist says temporary U.S.-China tariff deal doesn't ease uncertainty
rows.standfirst: Businesses are rushing to import Chinese goods after the U.S. struck a temporary deal. This "stop-go" nature of trade could still mean higher prices and doesn't ease uncertainty, an economist warns.

rows.title: Why aren't Americans filling the manufacturing jobs we already have?
rows.standfirst: Leaders from both major political parties have been working to bring back manufacturing. But American manufacturers say they are struggling to fill the manufacturing jobs we already have.

rows.title: First, relief. Then, a scramble to get stuff in after U.S. cuts China tariffs for now
rows.standfirst: Although business owners welcomed a temporary deal with China to slash tariffs, there's still considerable uncertainty about what happens next.

rows.title: A brief history of NPR funding
rows.standfirst: Where does NPR get its funding? Today on the show, we open our books and share a brief history of public radio. And we learn what's at stake with President Trump's executive order to cut off federal funding to NPR.

rows.title: Trump tried to fire Corporation for Public Broadcasting board members. Then came DOGE
rows.standfirst: DOGE staffers tried to assign a team to the independent Corporation for Public Broadcasting after President Trump's purported firing of three board members last month.

rows.title: Stocks soar after U.S. and China agree to temporarily slash tariffs
rows.standfirst: Stocks rallied after the U.S. and China said they would slash tariffs on each other's imports for 90 days.

rows.title: Trump tried to shutter Radio Free Europe. The EU threw it a lifeline
rows.standfirst: The Trump administration is withholding $75 million designated for the news outlet. EU officials say RFE/RL has played a critical role in providing news to areas where the press can't operate freely.

rows.title: How economists (and TikTok) know if a recession is coming
rows.standfirst: Lately we've noticed that something we think about all the time here at Planet Money is having a viral moment: recession indicators!

rows.title: A Newark air traffic controller on the moment systems went dark
rows.standfirst: Federal regulators are now limiting the number of flights in and out of Newark Liberty International Airport. This comes after a harrowing month for the air traffic controllers who work the airspace around it.

rows.title: Can retailers eat tariffs without price hikes? Walmart, Target, Lowe's face pressure
rows.standfirst: Major chains are fighting two battles at once: a financial battle to keep costs low in the face of new tariffs, and a political one to avoid the president's wrath.

rows.title: Homebuyers and sellers say agents' cuts are too big. Flat-fee brokers offer an alternative
rows.standfirst: Agents have typically taken a commission on the sale of a home that totals 5% to 6% of the price. But new rules have created an opening for brokers who charge much less.

rows.title: The great battery race: China and the U.S. compete over the future of EVs
rows.standfirst: The car you drive years in the future might run off a battery being invented in a lab today. Companies in China and the United States are racing to perfect and scale up next-generation technologies.

rows.title: The old trade war that brought foreign carmakers to the U.S.
rows.standfirst: President Donald Trump wants more products made in America, and he's not afraid of a few trade wars to make it happen. Back in the 80s, a different trade dispute brought new manufacturing to the U.S. Today on the show, how former President Ronald Reagan used the threat of trade protectionism to bring car-making stateside, and why the same strategy might not work today.

rows.title: Advice for navigating a volatile economy
rows.standfirst: The U.S. economy is in flux. And for millions of Americans, a new line item in their budget includes repaying federal student loans.

rows.title: How an AI-generated summer reading list got published in major newspapers
rows.standfirst: Newspapers around the country, including the Chicago Sun-Times and at least one edition of The Philadelphia Inquirer, published a syndicated book list featuring made-up books by famous authors.

rows.title: Home Depot doesn't plan to raise prices due to tariffs. But some items may disappear
rows.standfirst: The home improvement chain broke from many other retailers, who say they cannot afford to absorb new tariffs. President Trump recently attacked Walmart for warning of price hikes.

rows.title: Trump has imposed a lot of tariffs. But here's why collecting them can be hard
rows.standfirst: Collecting Trump's tariffs could be tricky. The agencies that screen imports say they're frequently overwhelmed and understaffed, and experts say exporters are becoming cannier at evading taxes.

rows.title: What a Texas showerhead salesman discovered about 'Made in the USA' labels
rows.standfirst: A Texas showerhead salesman wanted to know how much more customers would pay to buy a product that's made in the USA. The answer could pour cold water on President Trump's plan to encourage more companies to open factories in the U.S.

rows.title: The rise of the credit card airport lounge
rows.standfirst: We are back to answer your questions, listeners. Today on the show, we tackle three big questions: Are airport lounges worth it for credit card companies? How effective have carbon taxes been for Canada? Why is gasoline getting more expensive over the last few months as the price of crude oil has sunk?

rows.title: President of CBS News resigns as Trump lawsuit hovers over network
rows.standfirst: CBS News President Wendy McMahon says she's resigning because "the company and I do not agree on the path forward." CBS' parent company is trying to settle a lawsuit with President Trump.

rows.title: How President Trump is sparking a crypto revolution in America
rows.standfirst: Crypto exchange giant Coinbase is set to join the S&P 500 on Monday. It's the latest stunning development as Trump completely revamps the approach to crypto in the U.S.

rows.title: Meta plans to replace humans with AI to assess privacy and societal risks
rows.standfirst: Current and former Meta employees fear the new automation push comes at the cost of allowing AI to make tricky determinations about how Meta's apps could lead to real world harm.

rows.title: The U.S.-China trade war, according to game theory
rows.standfirst: Over the last few months U.S.-China trade relations have been pretty hard to make sense of – unless you look at what's happening through the lens of game theory. Game theory is all about how decisions are made, based not just on one side's options and payoffs, but on the choices and incentives of others.

rows.title: PBS and Minnesota public TV station sue Trump White House
rows.standfirst: PBS and Lakeland PBS in rural Minnesota are suing President Trump over his executive order demanding that the Corporation for Public Broadcasting kill all funding for the public television network.

rows.title: Trump to celebrate U.S. Steel deal with Japan. And, what's next for DOGE
rows.standfirst: President Trump is heading to Pittsburgh today to celebrate U.S. Steel and Nippon Steel's partnership. And, what's next for DOGE after Elon Musk's exit.

rows.title: Oil companies face a wrongful death suit tied to climate change
rows.standfirst: Julie Leon died of hyperthermia in Seattle on June 28, 2021 — the hottest day in the city's history. A lawsuit claims she was a victim of oil companies' "misrepresentations" about climate change.

rows.title: Sellers of dog leashes and mom gear hope court rulings lead to tariff relief
rows.standfirst: Court rulings against President Trump's tariffs could spell relief for many American importers — if the decisions hold. For now, the uncertainty remains.

rows.title: Anyone can use AI chatbots to 'vibe code.' Could that put programmers out of a job?
rows.standfirst: You no longer need to be a software engineer to build software — you can "vibe code" it by prompting chatbots to build apps and websites. Could that put programmers out of a job?

rows.title: Exodus of USDA veterinarians and others drives fears that U.S. farms are at risk
rows.standfirst: More than a thousand people who worked to keep American agriculture free of pests and disease have left the federal workforce in President Trump's massive government downsizing.

rows.title: Market Basket CEO is put on leave in new spat at family-controlled supermarket chain
rows.standfirst: The board alleges that CEO Arthur T. Demoulas has been planning a work stoppage at the Massachusetts-based retailer. It also says he has "resisted an appropriate succession plan for Market Basket."

rows.title: World financial markets welcome court ruling against Trump's tariffs
rows.standfirst: Financial markets welcomed a U.S. court ruling that blocks President Trump from imposing sweeping tariffs on imports under an emergency-powers law.

rows.title: Are Trump's trade deals the real deal?
rows.standfirst: Top Trump advisers have been boasting about 'awesome' trade deals the administration is negotiating with other countries. But are these deals real ? Today on the show, we ask a former U.S. trade negotiator whether these agreements hold up.

rows.title: Federal court keeps Trump tariffs in place — for now
rows.standfirst: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit granted the Trump administration's request to temporarily put on hold the New York-based Court of International Trade judgment that struck down President Trump's tariffs.

rows.title: 'We're in a holding pattern': Home sales and building slump in the face of uncertainty
rows.standfirst: Would-be homebuyers are finding lots of reasons to wait.

rows.title: Why are college coaches paid so much?
rows.standfirst: If you had to guess, would you say the president of a university usually makes more money than the football coach? Well, you may be wrong. A college's football coach is often their highest paid employee. The University of Alabama pays its football coach on average close to $11 million. Today on the show, why are college football coaches paid so much? Do their salaries really make economic sense?

rows.title: Despite the pause on high tariffs, Chinese factories still face high uncertainty
rows.standfirst: A 90-day pause on triple-digit U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods has left exporters and importers in a high state of uncertainty. Factory owners in China tell NPR that orders are down overall.

frame: Up to15 visible Business-archive cards at four fixed weekly endpoints, restricted to each block; not a full-publication census
